Restoring a hand-cranked press

When I first started restoring the old press in my grandfather's barn, I assumed the hardest part would be finding replacement rollers, but the real challenge turned out to be the ink itself. Modern formulations dry far too quickly for a hand-cranked machine, so every impression smeared before the paper even left the bed. After three months of failed batches I finally mixed a slow oil base from linseed and stand oil, and the very first proof came off the press with edges so crisp I nearly framed it on the spot.

That matches my experience almost exactly. The trick nobody writes down is warming the plate before the first pass; a cold plate pulls the oil out of the ink and leaves a ghost image on the second sheet. I keep a heat lamp clamped to the frame now and the difference is night and day, even in a drafty workshop in the middle of winter.

For anyone following along at home, the linseed mix ratio that finally worked for me was three parts stand oil to one part raw linseed, cut with a drop of clove oil to slow the skinning. It smells like a dentist's office but the open time stretches to nearly twenty minutes, which is plenty for a careful two-color run.
